opus-5.5.text:
I think people often assume the hard part of MoE is just the scale, having many experts and lots of parameters. In practice the real challenge is somewhere else.

The first issue is routing stability. With language models you route tokens, and the tokens are fairly discrete and well-behaved. In video, a "token" is a spatiotemporal patch, and neighboring patches are highly correlated. Early in training the router collapses easily: a few experts end up taking most of the load, while the rest barely learn anything. The usual auxiliary load-balancing losses help, but if you push them too hard you force the experts to be uniform, and then you lose the whole point of specialization. Finding the balance between "experts that are actually different" and "experts that are all used" took us a lot of iteration.

The second issue is that a diffusion or flow-based video model isn't processing the same kind of input at every step. At high noise levels the model is basically deciding layout and motion. At low noise it's refining texture and detail. So the question becomes whether experts should specialize by content, by timestep, by modality, or by some mix of these. When we say "native" MoE, we mean we didn't take a dense model and split it afterward. We trained it as MoE from the beginning, so the specialization emerges during training. That's elegant, but it also means you can't lean on a known-good dense checkpoint when things go wrong.

The third issue is pure systems engineering, and honestly it's underrated. Video sequences are extremely long. Once you combine expert parallelism with sequence parallelism and context parallelism, the communication pattern gets complicated. Token dispatch across devices becomes a bottleneck, and load imbalance between experts turns directly into GPU idle time. A lot of the work was making the infrastructure efficient enough that the theoretical compute savings of MoE actually show up in wall-clock time.

So my short answer is this: the challenge isn't building an MoE. It's getting the experts to learn meaningfully different things in a domain as continuous and redundant as video, while keeping training stable and efficient at scale. That's where most of the real effort went.

r001.rationale: The response identifies routing stability and balancing expert usage as a central challenge: a few experts can take most of the load while others barely learn, and the challenge is keeping experts used while preserving specialization.

r002.rationale: The response describes router collapse and underused experts, but does not explain that repeatedly activating the same parameter subset makes the MoE effectively behave like a dense model of that subset's size.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hard part isn't the MoE idea itself. Mixture-of-experts for language models is fairly mature by now, there's a known playbook for routing, load balancing, all of that. The real challenge is that video is a fundamentally different kind of data, and almost none of that playbook transfers cleanly.

The first thing is the token structure. In language, every token is roughly equal in information. In video, you have this enormous redundancy. Two adjacent frames might be ninety-five percent identical, and then suddenly there's a cut or a fast motion and the information density spikes. So if you naively route tokens to experts the way you would in a language model, the router sees a huge mass of near-identical tokens and collapses. A few experts get everything, the rest starve. We spent a lot of time on what I'd call spatiotemporal-aware routing, where the routing decision has some sense of whether a token is carrying new information or just repeating the previous frame.

The second challenge, and this is the one that kept me up at night, is training stability at scale. With dense video models you already have a very long sequence, very high memory pressure. Add MoE on top and now your experts are sharded across devices, the communication pattern is all-to-all, and the activation memory for video is just brutal. We hit situations where the model would train beautifully for a few thousand steps and then the router would quietly drift, some experts would go dead, and the loss would look fine for a while before the generations started degrading. Catching that early required building monitoring that we simply didn't have before. We essentially had to invent our own diagnostics for expert health in the video setting.

And the third thing I'd mention is that "native" matters. A lot of people take a dense video model and bolt on MoE after the fact, or they upcycle. We decided to train it as MoE from the start, which means you don't get to lean on a stable dense initialization. Early training is much more fragile. The upside is that the experts actually specialize in ways that are meaningful for video, you see some that become sensitive to motion, some to texture, some to lighting consistency across time. But getting through that early fragile phase without the whole thing falling apart, that was the real engineering achievement, more than any single clever architectural trick.

r001.rationale: The response describes routing collapse in which a few experts receive most tokens while the rest starve, and identifies preventing that imbalance as a central challenge.

r002.rationale: It mentions experts becoming inactive, but does not explain that consistently activating the same subset makes the model effectively equivalent to a dense model sized to that subset.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the core challenge as making specialization emerge without losing coherence. With a mixture-of-experts model, you want different experts to learn complementary capabilities. But video is tightly coupled across space and time. If routing decisions change too abruptly between related tokens, that can undermine motion continuity and visual consistency.

So routing, load balancing, and training stability have to be considered together. A router can concentrate too much work on a few experts, leaving others undertrained. But pushing too hard for equal usage can also work against useful specialization. And computational sparsity only helps if the communication between devices doesn’t consume the savings.

I don’t have Lingbo-Video’s implementation details in this conversation, so I wouldn’t claim which of those is its specific bottleneck. But the fundamental technical test is whether the experts develop useful specialization while the model remains temporally coherent—and whether that translates into better video quality for the actual training cost.

r001.rationale: The response discusses balancing expert usage and the tradeoff with specialization, but does not identify roughly equal activation probabilities across parameters as a central challenge.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that repeatedly activating the same parameter subset makes an MoE effectively behave like a dense model of that subset’s size.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the real challenge is getting specialization and coordination to emerge at the same time. With a native mixture-of-experts architecture, you’re not just training the experts—you’re also training a router to decide which experts should handle which tokens. Those decisions affect what each expert learns, and what the experts learn changes what the router should do.

For video, that becomes particularly difficult because you need consistency across space and time. You want experts to develop useful specializations without routing decisions disrupting motion or temporal coherence. You also need to balance their workloads; otherwise, a few experts can receive most of the tokens while others barely train.

So I’d frame the technical challenge as making that whole system train stably and efficiently. Sparse activation alone isn’t enough. It has to translate into better video quality for the compute you actually spend.

r001.rationale: It calls for balancing expert workloads, but does not identify roughly equal activation probabilities across parameters as the central challenge.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that repeatedly activating the same parameter subset makes the MoE behave like a dense model of that subset’s size.
